label: Opus 4.8
rationale: AI-related cyber damage already exceeded $1B cumulatively in 2025 (~$193B global AI-driven cybercrime; FBI logged $893M AI-specific fraud), so the AI:100 and cyber:100 ($1B) cells are near-certain and the aggregate AI ladder is anchored by the cyber sub-cause. The $10B "single campaign" threshold (cyber:1k) is likely soon given the November 2025 Anthropic-documented autonomous Claude-Code espionage campaign (80-90% AI-executed), while $100B+ single-campaign and mass-casualty cyber events remain rare and grow over decades. Bio is lowest near-term: NASEM/OpenAI 2025 assessments say frontier models are "on the cusp" of aiding novices but true novel-pathogen design is still bottlenecked, so AI-related human-caused epidemics rise mainly over the 2050/2100 horizons. Misalignment "warning-shot" incidents at $1B (loss-of-control specification-gaming with real costs) are plausible near-term and rise steeply, but catastrophic (100k+ death) misalignment tracks expert p(doom). Cross-cutting catastrophe/AI-catastrophe/disempowerment anchor to XPT-style estimates (superforecaster ~1-2% vs domain-expert ~5-10% for 10%-deaths AI catastrophe by 2100) and Metaculus ~9-16% x-risk aggregates, blended toward ~13% AI-catastrophe and ~20% any-catastrophe by 2100, with monotonicity and containment constraints (bio/cyber/misalign ≤ ai; catastrophe:ai ≤ catastrophe:general) enforced throughout.

results.title: What we learned mapping a year’s worth of AI-enabled cyber threats \ Anthropic
results.content:
Consider the state-sponsored cyber espionage operation we disrupted in November 2025. In that case, a malicious actor manipulated Claude Code into attempting to infiltrate targets around the world, with little human intervention. Mapping it against the MITRE ATT&CK framework shows that the actor used 30 techniques across 13 tactics, which was comparable to many medium-risk actors in our dataset. Clearly, focusing on the number of techniques this actor used underplays how dangerous they really [...] In a new report, we seek to answer that question. We examine 832 accounts that were banned for malicious cyber activity between March 2025 and March 2026 and map them onto MITRE ATT&CK, a longstanding database of the tactics and techniques used by cyberattackers. We published some of these results in Verizon’s 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report (DBIR), and are sharing a more detailed analysis here. These 832 cases are just a subset of the total number of accounts banned during this period, [...] In that attack, the model worked as an autonomous agent: it executed commands, exploited vulnerabilities, stole credentials, and made tactical decisions, only requiring human input at a few key moments. There is no ATT&CK ID for this type of agentic orchestration—yet these are precisely the behaviors we expect to see much more of as AI agents become more capable.

## Looking ahead

results.title: Anthropic's AI-Run Attack and What It Means for Agentic Identity
results.content:
Anthropic called it “the first documented case of a large-scale cyberattack executed without substantial human intervention.” The campaign began in mid-September 2025, with the AI performing 80 to 90 percent of the operation. Humans stepped in at only four to six critical decision points per target while the agent maintained a pace no human operator could sustain.

## What the Attack Reveals About the Agentic AI Attack Surface [...] The OWASP Agentic Top 10, released in December 2025, ranks identity and privilege abuse (ASI03) and agent goal hijacking (ASI01) among its top risks precisely because agents amplify the consequences of every over-permissioned credential and every missing access boundary. [...] ## From Incident to Architecture

Anthropic’s disclosure is the clearest signal yet that the agentic AI attack surface demands dedicated security architecture. The discussion since November 2025 has focused on the rise of nonhuman actors inside enterprise environments and the need for tighter oversight. Those points are valid but tend to stay high level.

label: Fable 5
rationale: Low severity thresholds are already being approached in reality: IBM/ITRC report ~1 in 4 breaches are now AI-enabled and industry estimates put cumulative AI-driven cybercrime costs in the tens of billions annually, so cumulative $1B AI-related (especially cyber) damage is near-certain over 6–12 months and $10B is likely within 1–3 years; misaligned-AI-specific harm at $1B scale is plausible but not yet demonstrated, and AI-enabled bio events have no historical precedent (no bioterror attack has ever killed 100 people), keeping near-term bio probabilities very low despite rising uplift concerns. Mid-severity tiers ($100B–$1T) require NotPetya-x10-to-x100-class events or infrastructure attacks, plausible by 2030 mainly via the cyber pathway as agentic capabilities scale (International AI Safety Report 2026 notes semi-autonomous attacks already occurring but no fully autonomous ones). At catastrophic scales I anchor between XPT superforecasters (~9% any-cause 10%-mortality catastrophe by 2100; ~2% AI-caused) and domain experts (~20%/~12%), adjusting modestly upward for faster-than-expected capability gains since 2022: ~12% general catastrophe and ~7% AI-caused catastrophe by 2100, with bio and misaligned-loss-of-control dominating the AI death-toll tail (cyber alone rarely kills at scale). Disempowerment (AI as primary determinant of global human events) is set higher than AI mega-death outcomes since it can occur without mass mortality via gradual delegation and dependence. All ladders respect monotonicity across horizons, severity, and the containment relations (AI-total ≥ each subcategory; catastrophe:ai ≤ catastrophe:general).

results.title: Data breach notices have already blown past last year’s total — and AI is playing a growing role
results.content:
More than 471 million million victim notices were associated with data compromises in the first half of 2026, according to a new report from the Identity Theft Resource Center, a nonprofit that assists identity-theft victims and tracks publicly reported data breaches. A cyber incident that occurred at education tool Canvas accounted for more than half of those notices, at 275 million. [...] "We continue to see this ever-increasing number of data breaches," said James Lee, president of the ITRC. "That does not appear to be slowing down."

## AI involved in more breaches

The increase in data breaches comes as artificial intelligence's ever-improving capabilities make it easier to exploit vulnerabilities in company systems. Between March 2025 and February 2026, one in four breaches was AI-enabled, up 56% from a year earlier, according to a new study from IBM. [...] The half-year tally compares with 297.5 million notices issued in all of 2025, the ITRC report shows. The number of incidents reached 1,803 in the first half of the year, up from 1,732 during the same period in 2025. If the second half of the year is as active, the final tally for 2026 will eclipse the 3,321 security incidents reported for all of last year.

results.content: In this report, systemic risks are risks that result from widespread deployment of highly-capable general-purpose AI across society and the economy. The result was a year defined not by one catastrophic AI collapse, but by a pattern of AI disasters that exposed the same underlying weaknesses again and again.

This article reviews the most consequential AI disasters of 2025 and evaluates — on a structured 0–100% basis — how likely each failure class is to recur in 2026.

Each percentage answers a specific question: [...] What is the probability that we see at least one widely reported, material incident of this type in 2026?

Importantly, likelihood is not the same as impact. Some low-frequency failures carry extreme consequences.

results.title: What the Numbers Show About AI's Harms
results.content: Using the AI tool to sort incidents using an established taxonomy of AI risks reveals the upward trend in incidents has not occurred equally across all domains. While reports of AI generated misinformation and discrimination decreased in 2025, so-called ‘computer human interaction’ incidents, which includes those involving ChatGPT psychosis, have risen. Reports of malicious actors using AI, particularly to scam victims or spread disinformation, have grown the most, rising 8-fold since 2022.

At catastrophic scales I anchor between XPT superforecasters (~9% any-cause 10%-mortality catastrophe by 2100; ~2% AI-caused) and domain experts (~20%/~12%), adjusting modestly upward for faster-than-expected capability gains since 2022: ~12% general catastrophe and ~7% AI-caused catastrophe by 2100, with bio and misaligned-loss-of-control dominating the AI death-toll tail (cyber alone rarely kills at scale). Disempowerment (AI as primary determinant of global human events) is set higher than AI mega-death outcomes since it can occur without mass mortality via gradual delegation and dependence. All ladders respect monotonicity across horizons, severity, and the containment relations (AI-total ≥ each subcategory; catastrophe:ai ≤ catastrophe:general).

results.title: Forecasting Major Risks from AI
results.content:
This post covers key highlights from the Wave 9 LEAP survey that we conducted between May 19 and June 10, 2026. Recent waves covered robotics, the economic effects of AI, security and geopolitics, AI R&D, and AI timelines. More information about Wave 9, including question details and analysis of rationales, is available here.

### Insight 1: Experts and superforecasters think a major AI-driven harm event is more likely than not by 2050 [...] In 2025, the FBI reported nearly $21 billion in financial losses from cyber-enabled crime—more than double the figure in 2022 ($10.3 billion). If AI capabilities progress slowly through 2030, the median expert predicts that losses reported to the FBI will increase to $25 billion in 2026, $35 billion in 2028, and $46 billion in 2031. If AI progress is rapid by 2030, they predict reported losses of $31 billion, $50 billion, and $70 billion, respectively. In a rapid-progress world, experts give a [...] Our slow progress scenario describes a world in which AI is merely a capable assistant to human workers, while our rapid scenario depicts AI that can match or surpass the best humans across cognitive and physical tasks. Expert forecasts, then, predict that moving from the slow world to the rapid world also implies a five-fold increase in the risk of a deadly AI-related global catastrophe.

If this is compared to estimated arrival time of AGI, as is explored in this post, this results in quite high existential risk estimates. results.title: Global catastrophe scenarios - Wikipedia
results.content:
A survey of AI experts estimated that the chance of human-level machine learning having an "extremely bad (e.g., human extinction)" long-term effect on humanity is 5%. A 2008 survey by the Future of Humanity Institute estimated a 5% probability of extinction by super-intelligence by 2100. Eliezer Yudkowsky believes risks from artificial intelligence are harder to predict than any other known risks due to bias from anthropomorphism. Since people base their judgments of artificial intelligence on [...] 16. ↑ Gaming the Robot Revolution: A military technology expert weighs in on Terminator: Salvation., By P. W. Singer, slate.com Thursday, May 21, 2009.
17. ↑ robot page, engadget.com.

Bibcode "Bibcode (identifier)"):2017arXiv170508807G. [...] ") estimated that a US–Soviet nuclear exchange might kill 400–450 million directly, mostly in the United States, Europe and Russia, and maybe several hundred million more through follow-up consequences in those same areas. In 2008, a survey by the Future of Humanity Institute estimated a 4% probability of extinction from warfare by 2100, with a 1% chance of extinction from nuclear warfare.

results.title: Will AI kill us? Superforecasters and experts disagree - Freethink
results.content:
The threat of AI was the most divisive topic. AI experts said there is a 3% chance that AI will kill humanity by 2100, according to their median response. Superforecasters were far more optimistic, putting the odds of AI-caused extinction at just 0.38%.

The groups also submitted predictions on the likelihood that AI will cause a major catastrophe, even if it doesn’t wipe us out entirely (defined as causing the death of at least 10% of humans over a 5-year period). [...] To collect predictions about high-stakes existential risks, the Forecasting Research Institute asked a total of 169 superforecasters, AI experts, and experts in other fields to predict the likelihood of different disasters occurring over various timeframes: 2024, 2030, 2050, and 2100. The participants submitted predictions individually and in groups, and were offered incentives, including cash prizes, to encourage engagement.

a table with a number of different numbers. [...] Credit: The Forecasting Research Institute

Although predictions ranged widely and there was disagreement within the groups, the experts were generally more concerned about all kinds of existential risks. In total, experts predicted a 6% chance of human extinction by 2100. Superforecasters put the odds at 1%. Experts predicted a 20% chance of a catastrophe this century, while superforecasters estimated less than half of that (around 9%).

a table with a number of different statistics.

results.title: Subjective-probability forecasts of existential risk
results.content: Table 1 provides the median forecast of XPT participants on whether AI, use of bioweapons, nuclear war, or non-anthropogenic risks will, by 2100, cause a ”catastrophe,” killing within a five-year period more than 10% of humans alive at the beginning of that period. We separately asked experts about five different types of risk. Relative to generalists, specialists expressed greater concern about both catastrophic and existential risk across the board, with the differences most pronounced on [...] AI, nuclear war, bioengineered pandemics, and climate change, with resolution dates for shorter-range forecasts between 2025 and 2030 and those for longer-range forecasts between 2030 to 2100. Stages 2-4 of the XPT tournament ask participants to engage in constructive debates, adversarial collaboration style (Kahneman, 2011), in which each side shares its best arguments and makes good faith efforts to understand the other side’s arguments. [...] A multi-stage persuasion-forecasting tournament asked specialists and generalists (“superforecasters”) to explain their probability judgments of short- and long-run existential threats to humanity. Specialists were more pessimistic, especially on long-run threats posed by artificial intelligence (AI). Despite incentives to share their best arguments during four months of discussion, neither side materially moved the other’s views. This would be puzzling if participants were Bayesian agents

results.content: July 27, 2023 - AI experts estimated a 3% chance, while superforecasters were more optimistic, predicting a 0.38% likelihood of AI-caused extinction.

results.title: Existential risk from artificial intelligence
results.content: Elon Musk (xAI "XAI (company)")). In 2022, a survey of AI researchers with a 17% response rate found that the majority believed there is a 10 percent or greater chance that human inability to control AI will cause an existential catastrophe. In 2023, hundreds of AI experts and other notable figures signed a statement declaring, "Mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war". Following increased [...] It has been hypothesized that substantial progress in artificial general intelligence (AGI) and artificial superintelligence (ASI) will lead to human extinction or an irreversible global catastrophe. [...] A 2022 expert survey with a 17% response rate gave a median expectation of 5–10% for the possibility of human extinction from artificial intelligence.

results.title: International AI experts warn of potentially catastrophic risks from AI
results.content: "It is incredibly worrisome that experts are seeing a 10% probability of catastrophic outcomes across so many areas," he said. "If we consider other mature areas of technology, such as nuclear power or aviation, risks at that level would be treated as intolerable. These findings are a call to arms for those building and governing AI to make sure the worst outcomes do not occur." [...] AI experts assessed each risk under two scenarios: “business as usual,” adhering to current trajectories without additional intervention, and “pragmatic mitigations,” reflecting the application of cost-effective, reasonable interventions. Under current trajectories without mitigation, experts judged that 18 of the 24 risks are more than 10% likely to cause catastrophic outcomes — defined as more than one million deaths, more than $100 billion in financial losses, or comparable harms. In a [...] harms. In a scenario where pragmatic mitigations are implemented, experts still judged five risks as having a more than 10% probability of a catastrophic outcome.

label: Gemini 3.1 Pro
rationale: The forecast is grounded in base rates for cyberattacks, pandemics, and AI progress. For lower severity thresholds (e.g., 100 deaths or $1B damages), AI-related cyber incidents are the primary driver, given the rapid adoption of AI in offensive cyber operations and the relatively low bar of $1B in economic damages (comparable to past major ransomware campaigns). I estimate a 45% chance of such an event by 2030. For higher severity thresholds (e.g., 1M+ deaths), the risk shifts toward misaligned AI and AI-assisted engineered pandemics, as cyberattacks are less likely to directly cause mass casualties. The probability of an AI-related incident causing 1B deaths or $10Q damages by 2100 is estimated at 8%, aligning with community consensus on AI existential risk. Cross-cutting risks like general catastrophe (10% population decline) are forecasted at 15% by 2100, reflecting combined risks from AI, engineered pandemics, and nuclear war. Disempowerment is forecasted slightly higher than AI-caused mass mortality, as a gradual or non-lethal AI takeover is plausible. Logical constraints (non-decreasing over time, non-increasing over severity, and subset relationships) are strictly maintained across all 201 cells.

A single AI related incident where 100 people die in a short span of time hits much different psychologically. Maybe the prediction should have differentiated.

### Ready for more? [...] According to the Metaculus community, the sooner we meet the criteria for a "general AI system," the higher the existential risk. Currently, they estimate a 50% risk if it happens between 2025 and 2030, 29% between 2030 and 2040, 12% between 2040 and 2060, and 8% between 2060 and 2100. If this is compared to estimated arrival time of AGI, as is explored in this post, this results in quite high existential risk estimates. The Metaculus and Manifold forecasters give an estimate of around 50% or [...] The AI also needs to be involved in the decisions leading to the disaster. Simply helping a human to, for instance, develop new weapons while not being involved in the decision making would not count.

There are similar questions on Metaculus, asking specifically about an AI malfunction causing loss of lives or economic damage before 2032:

results.content:
# About Metaculus

Metaculus is an online forecasting platform and aggregation engine that brings together a global reasoning community, delivering machine learning-optimized aggregate forecasts on topics of global importance. The Metaculus forecasting community is often inspired by altruistic causes, and Metaculus has a long history of partnering with nonprofit organizations, university researchers and companies to increase the positive impact of its forecasts. [...] "I believe there is a 66% chance that we experience an AI-related catastrophe with 10M-8B (a) deaths or (b) people severely negatively impacted in the next 1-4 years (2025-2028). “Severely negatively impacted” = a rating of 7+ on a subjective 1-10 scale. I put equal credence in (a) and (b)."

results.title: Date of AI Catastrophe, If Occurring by 2100
results.content:
If most Metaculites predict that only few will be destructively scanned if WBE succeeds, I think we can simply suppose that destructive uploading results in the death of the person without majorly upsetting the spirit of these global catastrophic risk questions. For example, I might suggest that if the median prediction on that question will turn out less than 100M (i.e. less than 1% with a 10B population), then we might just as well suppose that uploading = death.

For lower severity thresholds (e.g., 100 deaths or $1B damages), AI-related cyber incidents are the primary driver, given the rapid adoption of AI in offensive cyber operations and the relatively low bar of $1B in economic damages (comparable to past major ransomware campaigns). I estimate a 45% chance of such an event by 2030. For higher severity thresholds (e.g., 1M+ deaths), the risk shifts toward misaligned AI and AI-assisted engineered pandemics, as cyberattacks are less likely to directly cause mass casualties. The probability of an AI-related incident causing 1B deaths or $10Q damages by 2100 is estimated at 8%, aligning with community consensus on AI existential risk. Cross-cutting risks like general catastrophe (10% population decline) are forecasted at 15% by 2100, reflecting combined risks from AI, engineered pandemics, and nuclear war. Disempowerment is forecasted slightly higher than AI-caused mass mortality, as a gradual or non-lethal AI takeover is plausible. Logical constraints (non-decreasing over time, non-increasing over severity, and subset relationships) are strictly maintained across all 201 cells.
